name: West Ridge

pitch_detail.notes: From the west ridge notch, climb steep blocks up onto the crest on excellent North Cascades granite.
The famous 'air step': an airy step/reach across a gap in the crest. Stay on the ridgeline, or drop left onto the north face if in doubt - none of it harder than easy 4th/5th class.
Work over or around a series of gendarmes and knife-edge sections, bypassing on the north or south side as the crest dictates.
Moderate, well-protected ridge climbing; efficient parties simul-climb this stretch.

The route's crux tower: an obvious steep step about two-thirds of the way up, climbed on its left side past a fixed piton. Stay left here to avoid drifting onto the harder West Ridge Direct variation.
Finish along the narrowing crest to a false summit, carefully downclimb about 10 ft of exposed rock, then make easy moves to the true summit.

rappel_detail.pull: Set the knot well clear of the lip and check the pull before committing.
rappel_detail.notes: Ridge rappel 1 of about 3. Downclimb from the summit back past the false summit to reach it.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural horn/block, top of the crux tower
hazards: The pull angles here are awkward and a rope that is not weighted cleanly off the horn can hang up. Watch the rope over the edge before the last person goes.
rappel_detail.station: On the crux tower at the top of the steep section, roughly 175 ft below the summit. Slings and cord are usually in place; it is the first station most parties use rather than downclimbing.

rappel_detail.notes: Ridge rappel 2 of about 3, landing on north-side snow.
hazards: The landing is on snow, and the step from rock to snow is where parties come off the rappel awkwardly. Have crampons and an axe ready before you start down.
rappel_detail.station: Below the crux tower, dropping onto snow on the north side of the ridge. Natural anchors: slung horns and blocks with accumulated tat, not a bolted station.

rappel_detail.notes: Ridge rappel 3 of about 3, back down to the notch between Forbidden and Torment. How many of the ridge steps you rappel rather than downclimb is up to the party.
hazards: Exposed downclimbing between stations. Stay roped on wet rock.
rappel_detail.station: On the lower ridge above the notch. Slung horn or block with tat; the 3rd/4th-class steps between here and the stations above are usually downclimbed.

rappel_detail.notes: Cat Scratch rappel 1 of about 5. Three parallel chimneys all go; parties most often use the one nearest the snow couloir.
hazards: Loose rock throughout. Rappel one at a time, and let each climber move out of the fall line before the next one pulls the rope.
rappel_detail.station: Top of the Cat Scratch gullies, the rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to reach it.

hazards: The rappel line follows fixed anchors on the small rib on the down-climber's left of the gullies. Parties that drift into the right-hand gully end up on loose ground with no stations, which is the descent error reported most often here.
rappel_detail.station: Next station down the same chimney, on the rib on the down-climber's left.

hazards: Some stations are deliberately short and easy to rappel straight past. Do not skip an anchor because you cannot yet see the next one.
rappel_detail.station: Mid-gully, on the rib on the down-climber's left.

rappel_detail.pull: Carry enough cord to build an extra station if you cannot find the next one.
hazards: Loose rock throughout. Rappel one at a time, and let each climber move out of the fall line before the next one pulls the rope.
rappel_detail.station: Lower gully, on the rib on the down-climber's left. This is the station most often reported as hard to find: if you cannot see it, stop and look on the rib before continuing.

rappel_detail.notes: Cat Scratch rappel 5 of about 5, landing on the snowfield. From here, reverse the glacier-remnant and talus traverse back to Boston Basin.
hazards: The moat where the snow pulls away from the rock reappears at the bottom and can need a step across or a short downclimb. Have crampons and an axe ready for the snow.
rappel_detail.station: Bottom of the gullies, above the snowfield below Forbidden's south face.

rappels: ~8 single-rope rappels: about 3 on the West Ridge back to the notch, mixed with downclimbing, then about 5 down the Cat Scratch gullies to the snowfield below the south face. Late season, expect one or two more in the gullies.
descent_text: There is no walk-off. Descend the way you came up as far as the notch, then take the rock gullies beside the couloir. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the West Ridge notch. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. Watch for the moat again at the bottom. From the base, reverse the glacier-remnant and talus traverse back to Boston Basin camp and out the climbers' trail to the trailhead. The descent is usually slower than the climb: parties report about 1.5 hours back down the ridge to the notch against about 1 hour up it.
approach: From the Boston Basin trailhead off Cascade River Road, follow the unsigned but well-beaten Boston Basin climbers' path. It starts by following the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about 1 mile, then splits off the roadbed to climb steeply and directly through forest. The trail crosses four seasonal creeks/streams (reliable water) as it switchbacks up through increasingly open timber, breaking out above treeline around 5,300 ft. Above treeline it continues into the broad boulder-and-heather Boston Basin cirque, past the usual high-camp sites around 6,300–6,600 ft (roughly 4–5 miles and 3–4 hours from the car, ringed by Sahale, Sharkfin Tower, and Mt. Torment). From camp, make an ascending traverse across talus and the Quien Sabe Glacier remnant toward Forbidden's south face; when the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is often a faster, drier alternative to crossing snow/ice. Rope up if the glacier is crevassed or snow-covered. Aim for the obvious ~500-ft snow-and-ice couloir splitting the left edge of the south face — the standard gully leading to the West Ridge notch. This couloir steepens to 40–50°+ near its top, typically wants crampons/axe (and sometimes a picket) into mid-summer, and is guarded by a moat near its top, against the rock walls approaching the notch, that can require a short steep step or a band of loose rock to surmount. Exiting the couloir at the ridge-crest notch is roughly 4–5 hours and about 4,500 ft above the trailhead.
overview: One of the Fifty Classic Climbs of North America and Forbidden's standard route: a sweeping, exposed arête of clean North Cascades granite. The crux is a single sustained 5.6 move near a prominent gendarme tower (stay left to avoid straying onto the harder West Ridge Direct variation), followed by a narrow knife-edge crest and a final false-summit downclimb — losing roughly 10 ft of elevation — before the true summit.
beta: Mostly 3rd/4th class scrambling with sustained exposure; the crux is a short steep step ("the Tower") about two-thirds up the ridge, climbed at 5.6 on its left side past a fixed piton. The first two or three pitches are often simul-climbed or soloed by experienced parties.
gear: single rack of cams to 2 inches
ice axe and crampons for the couloir
fa: Lloyd Anderson, Fred Beckey, Helmy Beckey, Jim Crooks, Dave Lind — June 1940 (also the peak's first ascent)
